title: 3 Principles for Keeping Questions Human
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: In a collaboration with Colette Molteni of Empathy Elevated, Chiarelli distinguishes asking questions to understand from asking questions to confirm what we already suspect. The piece uses a short narrative of a manager, Rahul, who drifts from curiosity into interrogation while questioning a junior colleague about flawed work, and shows how nearly identical wording can carry very different intent. Three principles follow: intent shapes the question before the words do, inquiry preserves the other person's agency while interrogation constrains it, and curiosity requires self-restraint. The key insight is that the slide into interrogation is a stress response under deadline pressure, not a character flaw, and that it costs the leader the full picture. The piece ends with a self-check question, am I trying to understand or to confirm, and short mini-prompts for each principle.
points: Confirmatory questions carry a hypothesis, while exploratory ones leave space for an explanation the leader has not yet considered.
Interrogation makes people shift from explaining to accounting, so the leader gets compliance and loses the full context.
Under pressure, narrowing the conversation feels like efficiency to the questioner but like being managed to the person answering.
Restraint, meaning fewer questions, silence and no interruptions, keeps curiosity useful instead of relentless.
A portable check, am I trying to understand or to confirm, tells a leader whether they are building trust or spending it.
quotes: This matters because most of us do not set out to interrogate our colleagues. We slide into it. A deadline tightens, a risk appears, our attention shifts from curiosity to containment, and suddenly we are steering the conversation rather than exploring it.
The thought is practical, but it changes his centre of gravity. He stops listening for understanding and starts scanning for risk.
The second question carries a hypothesis (it’s a confirmatory framing). The first makes space for one you haven’t yet considered (exploratory framing).

When we’re curious, the other person retains room to frame their thinking. When we shift into control, the questioner sets the track and the responder learns to stay on it. Once the person answering senses that the acceptable range has narrowed, they start managing exposure.
But curiosity has a failure mode: more questions do not automatically create more insight. When questioning becomes relentless or poorly timed, it starts to crowd out the exchange.

Rahul still has work to do, but he also has something better than compliance. He has clarity, and he knows exactly when it returned: the moment he stopped trying to confirm what he suspected, and gave the other person room to think out loud.
Next time you feel the impulse to interrogate rising, pause and ask: “Am I trying to understand, or am I trying to confirm?” The answer will tell you whether you are building trust or spending it.
